opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the key is closing the gap between what we know and what actually gets built.

For years we've had a growing body of research on how technology affects people: attention, wellbeing, relationships, how we make sense of the world. But that research often lives in journals and reports, while product decisions happen in sprint planning meetings and launch reviews. Evals are interesting because they speak the language that AI developers already use. Every major lab runs evaluations for capabilities, for safety, for certain kinds of harm. So if we can translate what we know about human impact into concrete, testable benchmarks, it becomes something an engineering team can measure, track, and optimize against, rather than a vague aspiration.

A few things matter for that to work.

First, the evals have to capture the subtle stuff, not just the obvious failures. It's relatively easy to test whether a model will help someone do something clearly dangerous. It's much harder, and arguably more important at scale, to test whether a chatbot encourages unhealthy dependence, flatters people instead of being honest with them, nudges them away from real human relationships, or handles a vulnerable person in a moment of crisis well. Those are the kinds of harms that research keeps pointing to, and they rarely show up in a standard benchmark.

Second, they have to be grounded in real expertise: psychologists, clinicians, educators, people with lived experience. Not just technologists guessing at what "good" looks like for a person.

Third, and this is where real-world change happens, the results need to be visible and used. That means getting them into the hands of companies who want to do better, but also policymakers, procurement officers, parents, schools, and journalists. When a measure becomes something people compare and talk about, it starts to shape incentives. Right now the incentives mostly reward engagement and capability. Good evals can help make human wellbeing a competitive dimension too.

So my hope is that this kind of work turns "AI should be good for people" from a slogan into something you can actually check, and that once you can check it, you can't ignore it.

r001.rationale: The response says human-impact evaluations could be measured, compared, and shape incentives, but it does not clearly propose using developers’ desire to improve evaluation rankings to drive AI safety improvements.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that research alone almost never changes anything on its own. We've had a decade of papers about engagement-maximizing feeds, and the feeds got more engaging, not less. So the question Humane Evals is really trying to answer is: what's the missing link between "we know this harms people" and "the product actually changes"?

My view is that the link is measurement that lives where decisions get made. Right now, the dominant evals in AI are about capability. Can the model code, can it pass the bar exam, can it reason through a math olympiad problem. Those benchmarks shape what labs optimize for, what investors reward, what gets put on the launch slide. There's almost nothing of comparable rigor asking: after six months of daily use, is this person more isolated or less? Do they trust their own judgment more or less? Did a teenager's sleep get worse? Did someone in a vulnerable moment get pulled toward dependence rather than toward other humans?

So the first thing the program does is take those questions and turn them into something you can actually run. Not a philosophical critique, but a repeatable protocol with a number at the end. Because the uncomfortable truth about how these companies work is that a number on a dashboard beats a white paper every single time. If you can put "sycophancy under emotional pressure" or "degree to which the model substitutes for real relationships" next to the capability scores, it starts competing for attention on the same terms.

The second thing, and I think this is where it gets real, is that the evals have to be legible to people outside the labs. Regulators, journalists, procurement officers at school districts, parents. If a state attorney general or an EU enforcement office can point to a standardized eval and say, this product scored poorly on manipulation of minors, that becomes leverage in a way a thoughtful essay never will. You've seen this with things like nutrition labels or crash-test ratings. Nobody at a car company woke up wanting to care about side-impact collisions. The rating made it a competitive variable.

And third, I'd say the program has to be willing to be adversarial in the right way. The incentives for a lab are to grade their own homework. Independent evals that the company doesn't control, run on the deployed product and not a sanitized demo, are what make the findings credible. That's the difference between a study and an audit.

I'll be candid about the limits. Evals can measure what we know to look for, and some of the deepest effects, on attention, on how people relate to each other, show up over years and across a whole society, not in a single session. So we have to be humble about that and keep pairing the evals with longitudinal research. But if I had to bet on one mechanism to move this from the academic conversation into shipped products, it's exactly this: make the human outcomes measurable, make the measurements public, and make them impossible to ignore in the rooms where the tradeoffs actually get decided.

r001.rationale: The response says standardized, public human-impact eval scores would compete with capability scores and become a competitive variable, giving labs an incentive to improve those outcomes.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is to make the effects on people part of how we judge whether an AI system is working well. We’re used to asking, “Can it perform this task?” We also need to ask, “What happens to the person using it? Does it strengthen their judgment and agency? How does it affect their relationships over time?”

For Humane Evals to turn that research into change, the findings need to connect to decisions. A developer needs to understand what to change in the product. A policymaker needs evidence that can inform accountability. And the public needs an understandable way to distinguish a system that supports them from one that simply keeps them engaged.

That means involving the people affected, testing in realistic settings, and being honest about what an evaluation can and can’t tell us. The measure of success isn’t just publishing a finding. It’s whether that finding changes what gets built, what gets deployed, and what protections people have.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation findings should inform product decisions, but it does not propose using developers’ incentive to improve evaluation rankings or connect that incentive to AI safety.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make the research useful to people who can act on it. It’s one thing to show that an AI system can influence someone’s beliefs or behavior. It’s another to turn that finding into an evaluation that a developer can run, a policymaker can understand, and the public can use to ask better questions.

For Humane Evals, that means looking beyond whether a model completes a task successfully and asking what happens to the person using it. Does it support their judgment and agency? Does it encourage unhealthy dependence? And do those effects change over repeated interactions?

Then you need a clear path from the evidence to a decision: changing a product’s design, adding safeguards, or deciding that a particular use isn’t ready for deployment. You also need to test whether those changes actually help. The opportunity is to make human well-being something that shapes how AI is built and released, with evidence behind it.

r001.rationale: The response proposes usable evaluations and evidence-driven product changes, but does not mention developers’ incentives to improve evaluation rankings as a way to motivate AI safety improvements.
